result: The study included 318 Tanzanian and 416 Dutch participants after quality control. Tanzanians were significantly older (median 30.2 vs 23.0 years, p<0.0001) and Tanzanian females had higher BMI than Dutch females (25.7 vs 21.5, p<0.0001).
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C89-C92, C107-C108 provide consistent demographic data with appropriate statistical testing and clear documentation of sample sizes and exclusion criteria. The age and BMI differences are supported by p-values and the data quality procedures are well-described.

result: Using the Olink 92-protein inflammation panel, 74 proteins were analyzed after excluding 18 proteins with >25% values below detection limit. PCA showed clear separation between cohorts, with 35 proteins significantly higher and 20 lower in Tanzanians (FDR p<0.05, adjusted for age, sex, BMI).
evaluation: Claims C4-C7, C93-C96, C104-C110 describe appropriate proteomic methodology with proper batch correction, quality control, and statistical analysis. The differential expression analysis used appropriate methods (Limma) with FDR correction and adjustment for confounders. Sample handling differences (freeze-thaw cycles) are acknowledged and cited as having limited impact.

result: The most upregulated proteins in Tanzanians were metabolic regulators 4E-BP1 (log2 FC 1.9, p=1.3×10⁻⁶⁰) and FGF21 (log2 FC 1.3, p=1.3×10⁻³⁰). FGF21 is an insulin sensitizer whose secretion increases with high carbohydrate/low protein intake, consistent with traditional Tanzanian diets, though no association with BMI was found.
evaluation: Claims C8-C11, C71-C79, C82, C113 provide strong statistical evidence for upregulation of 4E-BP1 and FGF21 with highly significant p-values. The biological interpretation is supported by citations to prior literature on FGF21 function and dietary regulation. The lack of BMI association (C79) is appropriately noted as contradicting some prior literature (C78).

result: Multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines were significantly upregulated in Tanzanians, including IL-17A, IL-17C, CC-chemokines (CCL11, CCL3, CCL7, CCL8), and cytokines (TNF, IL-6, IL-10, IL-18, OSM, ADA), all with highly significant p-values.
evaluation: Claims C12-C18 report differential expression of multiple inflammatory proteins with highly significant p-values (ranging from 10⁻¹⁰ to 10⁻⁷⁴) and appropriate fold changes. The statistical evidence is strong and consistent with the overall pro-inflammatory phenotype conclusion.

result: Tanzanians showed downregulation of AXIN1 (negative Wnt regulator, log2 FC -0.7, p=6.5×10⁻¹⁸) and upregulation of CDCP1 (Wnt promoter, log2 FC 0.7, p=1.8×10⁻⁶¹), suggesting enhanced Wnt/β-catenin pathway activity. This pathway is implicated in inflammatory diseases, diabetes, and cancer.
evaluation: Claims C19-C26, C83-C85, C112 provide strong statistical evidence for differential expression of Wnt pathway regulators with highly significant p-values. The inference of enhanced Wnt pathway activity (C26, C112) is reasonable based on the opposing regulation of a negative regulator (AXIN1) and positive regulator (CDCP1), supported by citations to pathway function.

result: Tanzanians had lower levels of CXC chemokines (CXCL1, CXCL5, CXCL6, CXCL8/IL8), which mediate neutrophil trafficking.
evaluation: Claims C27-C28 report downregulation of multiple CXC chemokines with appropriate functional context from cited literature. This finding is consistent with the overall differential inflammatory profile between cohorts.

result: Tanzanians had significantly higher plasma IL-1Ra, IL-6, IL-18, and leptin, with lower adiponectin than Dutch (adjusted for age, sex, BMI). Tanzanian females had higher leptin regardless of BMI, consistent with prior studies showing 50% higher leptin in Tanzanians. No differences were found in resistin or AAT.
evaluation: Claims C29-C32, C80-C81 report cytokine and adipokine measurements using orthogonal methods (ELLA platform, ELISA) that confirm and extend the Olink findings. The results are adjusted for confounders and consistent with prior literature (C80). The claim about ethnic differences in metabolic profiles (C81) is appropriately framed as an inference supported by citations.

result: In Dutch participants, advancing age was associated with increased inflammatory proteins (IL-6, IL-7, IL-18, MCP2-4, MMP1, IL-8, HGF), but these associations were largely absent in Tanzanians, except for CDCP1, CCL11, and CCL25. The reasons for lack of age-associated inflammation in Tanzanians remain uncertain.
evaluation: Claims C33-C36, C67-C70 describe differential age associations between cohorts with appropriate statistical analysis. The finding is supported by data and consistent with cited literature on aging in wealthy countries (C67). The acknowledgment of uncertainty (C69) and speculation about mechanisms (C70) are appropriately qualified.

result: Females in both cohorts had lower inflammatory protein concentrations than males overall, though Tanzanian females had higher TNF-beta, IL12-beta, and CCL28 than Tanzanian males.
evaluation: Claims C37-C38 report sex-stratified analyses showing general patterns and specific exceptions. The findings are consistent with prior work cited in the manuscript and represent appropriate subgroup analyses.

result: No significant associations were found between inflammatory proteins and environmental exposures (toilet type, wood smoke, farm animals, water access, infections, antibiotic use) in Tanzanians.
evaluation: Claims C39 and C66 report null findings for environmental exposure associations. While negative results, these are important for ruling out potential confounders of the diet-inflammation associations and are appropriately reported.

result: Unsupervised clustering of food-derived metabolites identified two clusters associated with dietary patterns (traditional vs Western). Inflammatory proteome clustering revealed two groups, with traditional diet cluster overrepresented in lower inflammation and Western diet cluster in higher inflammation. Age, sex, and season were not associated with inflammatory clustering.
evaluation: Claims C40-C45, C98-C103 describe metabolomics methodology and clustering analyses linking diet to inflammation. The metabolomics methods are appropriately described with limitations acknowledged (C101). The clustering approach is unsupervised and shows clear associations between dietary patterns and inflammatory profiles, though the metabolite identifications are pending LC-MS/MS validation.

result: Plant-derived polyphenols (apigenin, naringenin, gallic acid, etc.) showed negative associations with inflammatory proteins (especially MCP and CXCL families), while carboxylic acids and organooxygen compounds showed positive associations. Tanzanians consuming traditional foods (ugali, plantain, vegetables) had lower inflammatory proteins, supporting diet as an important driver of inflammation variation.
evaluation: Claims C46-C48, C60-C65, C54 describe metabolite-protein correlations and dietary associations with inflammation. The correlation analyses are appropriate and show consistent patterns. The conclusions about diet impact are supported by the data and consistent with prior work in the same cohort (C62-C63). The public health inference (C65) is appropriately framed as supported by the findings.

result: A 2-week dietary intervention switching from Western to traditional Tanzanian diet resulted in significant reductions in 4E-BP1 (β=-1.87, p=0.003) and FGF-19 (β=-1.253, p=0.0001), a trend toward AXIN1 reduction (β=-0.555, p=0.063), but no change in CDCP1 (β=0.049, p=0.464).
evaluation: Claims C49-C52 report preliminary data from a small dietary intervention (n=23 males) that partially supports the cross-sectional findings. While 4E-BP1 and FGF-19 changes are significant, AXIN1 is only a trend (p=0.063) and CDCP1 shows no change. The small sample size, short duration, male-only population, and preliminary nature limit the strength of these findings. This requires further validation with larger, more diverse samples.

result: Healthy Tanzanians display a more prominent pro-inflammatory phenotype compared to healthy Dutch individuals.
evaluation: Claims C53 and C111 represent the primary conclusion synthesizing the differential expression findings (C7-C18, C29-C30). This is well-supported by the extensive proteomic data showing 35 upregulated and 20 downregulated proteins with highly significant p-values, adjusted for confounders.

result: Prior work showed ancestry-specific genetic regulation of immune responses with interferon pathway enrichment in Tanzanians. Natural selection for strong inflammatory responses may have been advantageous historically in high infectious disease burden areas but may become disadvantageous with epidemiological transition and lifestyle changes, potentially driving NCDs.
evaluation: Claims C55, C128-C129 cite prior work in the same cohorts showing genetic differences. Claims C56-C59, C130 present evolutionary and epidemiological inferences that are appropriately qualified and supported by citations. These provide important context for interpreting the current findings but are not primary results of this study.

result: The findings reveal significant differences in inflammatory and metabolic proteins between East African and Western European populations, with important implications for the epidemiological transition in sub-Saharan Africa and the need to include underrepresented populations in systems immunology studies.
evaluation: Claims C86-C88, C114-C115 represent summary conclusions and broader implications. These are appropriately supported by the extensive data presented and represent reasonable inferences about the significance of the work for public health and research practices.

result: The introduction establishes that immune responses vary due to genetic and environmental factors, populations differ in inflammatory proteins, urbanization drives epidemiological transition, and non-Western populations are underrepresented in systems immunology research despite offering unique opportunities to understand NCDs.
evaluation: Claims C116-C127, C131-C134 provide background context supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These establish the rationale for the study and are appropriately framed as established knowledge or prior findings rather than new results.
